title: Job 26:1–4
context: Job answers Bildad (26:1). In 26:2–4 he speaks with biting irony, addressing Bildad directly: how has Bildad helped the powerless, saved the weak arm, or counseled the one without wisdom, and whose spirit has spoken through him? Job’s rebuke turns Bildad’s claim to wisdom back on him and suggests that the friends’ speeches have offered neither help nor comfort. The question “Whose spirit came out of you?” (26:4) may glance back at Eliphaz’s claim of a night vision (4:12–17), though that link is suggested rather than stated. Both Arminian and Reformed readers take these verses as Job’s honest protest against counsel that is correct in places but misapplied to him, and they read the rebuke as part of the book’s larger testing of the friends’ theology rather than as a model of sarcasm to imitate.

verses.arminianNotes: The narrator introduces Job’s reply to Bildad’s brief third speech. Arminian readers note that Job keeps answering, refusing to be silenced by the friends’ appeals to God’s majesty, and they see in his persistence a man who still believes that truth about his case matters to God and can be spoken before him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job maintaining his voice under pressure, and they note that the dialogue is now nearing its end, with the friends’ arguments thinning while Job’s speeches lengthen. Shared ground: both traditions take the formula as marking Job as the speaker of what follows, at least as the text stands.

verses.text: “How have you helped him who is without power! How have you saved the arm that has no strength!
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks with irony how Bildad has helped the powerless and saved the arm without strength. Arminian readers hear a rebuke of comfort that ignores the sufferer, and they stress that true care for the weak reflects God’s own heart for the afflicted (compare Psalm 72:12–13), which the friends have failed to show.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hear sharp irony and see Job naming a pastoral failure: sound statements about God offered without compassion have left the weak unhelped. Shared ground: both traditions draw from the verse a lesson about counsel that is doctrinally confident but pastorally empty, while hedging how much sarcasm Job intends.

verses.text: How have you counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge!
verses.arminianNotes: Job mocks the counsel given to one who has no wisdom and the plentiful sound knowledge declared. Arminian readers note that Job turns the friends’ repeated charge that he lacks wisdom (compare 15:2–3) back on them, and they see a reminder that wisdom must fit the actual situation of the person being counseled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job exposing the gap between the friends’ claim to wisdom and its fruit, a theme chapter 28 will take up when it asks where wisdom can be found. Shared ground: both traditions hold that true wisdom comes from God (compare 28:28) and that the friends’ abundance of words has not proved that they possess it.

verses.text: To whom have you uttered words? Whose spirit came out of you?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks to whom Bildad has spoken and whose spirit came out of him. Some readers hear a glance back at Eliphaz’s claim of a spirit in the night (4:15–16), though this is suggested rather than stated. Arminian readers see Job questioning whether the friends’ words truly come from God or merely repeat tradition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear Job challenging the source and authority of Bildad’s speech, and they note that claims to speak for God must be tested (compare 1 John 4:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the question as Job’s challenge to the friends’ authority, without settling whether a specific earlier claim is in view.
